CHAPTER 28 - CARBON AND ITS COMPOUNDS

Introduction

Carbon is one of the most remarkable elements known to us. Although it makes up only about 0.02% of the Earth's crust and a small fraction of the atmosphere (as carbon dioxide), it forms the backbone of all living matter. The number of compounds containing carbon runs into millions, far exceeding the compounds formed by all the other elements put together. The study of carbon compounds is so vast that a whole branch of chemistry - organic chemistry - is devoted to it. In this chapter we explore why carbon is so versatile, the different forms (allotropes) in which pure carbon exists, the families of hydrocarbons, functional groups and homologous series, the typical chemical reactions of carbon compounds, and two important compounds - ethanol and ethanoic acid - along with soaps and detergents.

28.1 CARBON - A VERSATILE ELEMENT

Carbon has the atomic number 6 and the electronic configuration 2, 4. It has four electrons in its outermost shell, so it needs four more electrons to complete its octet. Carbon could in principle either lose 4 electrons (forming C4+) or gain 4 electrons (forming C4-). Both options require a very large amount of energy and would leave a highly charged, unstable ion. Therefore carbon neither gains nor loses electrons - instead it SHARES its four valence electrons with other atoms. This sharing of electrons is called COVALENT BONDING, and the bonds formed are covalent bonds.

Because carbon has a valency of FOUR, it is said to be TETRAVALENT. It can form four covalent bonds with other atoms - with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, the halogens, and most importantly with other carbon atoms. The simplest example is methane (CH4), in which one carbon atom shares its four electrons with four hydrogen atoms, forming four single covalent bonds.

Two special properties make carbon uniquely able to form a huge number of compounds:
 (1) CATENATION - the ability of carbon atoms to link with one another through covalent bonds to form long chains, branched chains and rings. Because carbon-carbon bonds are strong and stable, these chains can contain dozens or even thousands of carbon atoms. No other element shows catenation to this extent (silicon shows it to a small degree).
 (2) TETRAVALENCY - having a valency of four, each carbon atom can bond to up to four other atoms, allowing complex three-dimensional structures.
In addition, carbon can form DOUBLE bonds (sharing two pairs of electrons) and TRIPLE bonds (sharing three pairs). Carbon also bonds strongly to many other elements. Together these features explain the millions of carbon compounds.

28.2 ALLOTROPES OF CARBON

Elements that exist in more than one physical form, having the same chemical properties but different physical properties, are said to show ALLOTROPY, and the different forms are called ALLOTROPES. Carbon has several allotropes; the important crystalline ones are diamond, graphite and fullerene.

 (a) DIAMOND - In diamond each carbon atom is bonded to FOUR other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds, forming a rigid three-dimensional network. This makes diamond the HARDEST natural substance known. It has a very high melting point. Because all four valence electrons of every carbon are used in bonding, no free electrons are available, so diamond does NOT conduct electricity. Diamond is used in cutting and drilling tools and as a gemstone.

 (b) GRAPHITE - In graphite each carbon atom is bonded to only THREE other carbon atoms, forming flat layers of hexagonal rings. The layers are held together by weak forces and can slide over one another, which makes graphite soft and slippery - hence its use as a lubricant and in pencil 'lead'. The fourth electron of each carbon is free to move, so graphite is a good CONDUCTOR of electricity. It is used as electrodes.

 (c) FULLERENE - Fullerenes are a newer class of carbon allotropes made of carbon atoms arranged in the shape of a hollow sphere or tube. The best known is C60 (buckminsterfullerene), which contains 60 carbon atoms arranged like the panels of a football (soccer ball). Fullerenes were discovered in 1985.

28.3 SATURATED AND UNSATURATED HYDROCARBONS

A HYDROCARBON is a compound made of only carbon and hydrogen. Hydrocarbons are of two broad types:
 - SATURATED hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms (C-C). The carbon atoms hold the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms. These are the ALKANES.
 - UNSATURATED hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C) or triple bond. Those with a double bond are ALKENES; those with a triple bond are ALKYNES.

28.4 ALKANES, ALKENES AND ALKYNES

ALKANES (general formula CnH2n+2) are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds. The first four members are:
 Methane  CH4   (n=1)
 Ethane   C2H6  (n=2)
 Propane  C3H8  (n=3)
 Butane   C4H10 (n=4)
In IUPAC naming, the number of carbon atoms is shown by the prefix (meth- 1, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4) and the ending '-ane' shows that it is an alkane.

ALKENES (general formula CnH2n) are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon DOUBLE bond. The simplest is ethene (C2H4, also called ethylene). The ending is '-ene'. Example: propene C3H6.

ALKYNES (general formula CnH2n-2) are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing one carbon-carbon TRIPLE bond. The simplest is ethyne (C2H2, also called acetylene). The ending is '-yne'. Ethyne is used in oxy-acetylene welding because it burns with a very hot flame.

28.5 ISOMERISM

Compounds that have the SAME molecular formula but DIFFERENT structural arrangements of atoms are called ISOMERS, and the phenomenon is called ISOMERISM. For example, butane C4H10 can exist as a straight chain (n-butane) or as a branched chain (isobutane). Both have the formula C4H10 but their atoms are joined differently, giving slightly different physical properties. The first three alkanes (methane, ethane, propane) have no isomers; isomerism begins at butane.

28.6 FUNCTIONAL GROUPS

A FUNCTIONAL GROUP is an atom or group of atoms that gives a carbon compound its characteristic chemical properties. When a hydrogen atom of a hydrocarbon is replaced by a functional group, the compound's behaviour changes. Important functional groups are:
 - Halo (-Cl, -Br): halogen compounds, e.g. chloromethane CH3Cl.
 - Alcohol (-OH, hydroxyl): e.g. ethanol C2H5OH.
 - Aldehyde (-CHO): e.g. ethanal CH3CHO.
 - Ketone (>C=O within the chain): e.g. propanone CH3COCH3 (acetone).
 - Carboxylic acid (-COOH): e.g. ethanoic acid CH3COOH.

28.7 HOMOLOGOUS SERIES

A HOMOLOGOUS SERIES is a family of carbon compounds having the same general formula and the same functional group, in which each successive member differs from the previous one by a -CH2- unit (that is, by CH2, a mass of 14). The members of a homologous series show a gradual change in physical properties (such as melting and boiling points) with increasing molecular mass, but they have similar chemical properties because they share the same functional group. The alkanes form a homologous series, as do the alkenes, the alkynes, the alcohols and the carboxylic acids.

28.8 CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF CARBON COMPOUNDS

 (1) COMBUSTION - Carbon and most carbon compounds burn in air (oxygen) to give carbon dioxide, water and heat. For example: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat. Saturated hydrocarbons generally burn with a clean blue flame, while unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a yellow, sooty (smoky) flame because of unburnt carbon particles.

 (2) OXIDATION - Some substances called oxidising agents (such as alkaline potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate) can add oxygen to a carbon compound. Ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid by such oxidising agents.

 (3) ADDITION REACTION - Unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes and alkynes) add hydrogen across the double or triple bond in the presence of a catalyst (nickel, palladium or platinum) to form saturated compounds. This is called HYDROGENATION. The industrial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (which contain unsaturated chains) converts them into solid fats (vanaspati / margarine) using a nickel catalyst.

 (4) SUBSTITUTION REACTION - In saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes), one or more hydrogen atoms can be replaced by another atom (such as chlorine) in the presence of sunlight. For example: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl (in sunlight). This is a substitution reaction.

28.9 IMPORTANT CARBON COMPOUNDS

ETHANOL (ethyl alcohol, C2H5OH) - Ethanol is a colourless liquid with a pleasant smell, soluble in water in all proportions. It is the alcohol present in alcoholic drinks. Properties and reactions: ethanol reacts with sodium to release hydrogen gas; on heating with concentrated sulphuric acid it undergoes dehydration to give ethene. Uses: as a solvent in medicines, tinctures and perfumes; as a raw material in industry; and increasingly as a FUEL. Ethanol is mixed with petrol to make 'gasohol', a cleaner-burning fuel; ethanol burns to give carbon dioxide and water releasing heat. However, consumption of ethanol affects the nervous system and excessive use is harmful to health.

ETHANOIC ACID (acetic acid, CH3COOH) - Ethanoic acid is a member of the carboxylic acid family. A 5-8% solution of ethanoic acid in water is called VINEGAR, used widely in pickles and cooking. Pure ethanoic acid freezes in cold weather (below 17 degrees C) and is therefore called GLACIAL ACETIC ACID. Properties and reactions: it is a weak acid; it turns blue litmus red; it reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) to give carbon dioxide gas, water and sodium acetate; it reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid catalyst to form a sweet-smelling ester (this reaction is called ESTERIFICATION). Esters are used in perfumes and flavourings.

28.10 SOAPS AND DETERGENTS

A SOAP is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid (a carboxylic acid). Soaps are made by heating fats or oils with sodium hydroxide - this process is called SAPONIFICATION. A soap molecule has two parts: a long hydrocarbon 'tail' that is HYDROPHOBIC (water-repelling, but oil/grease loving) and an ionic 'head' (-COONa) that is HYDROPHILIC (water-loving).

CLEANSING ACTION: When soap is added to water containing greasy dirt, the hydrophobic tails dissolve into the oil droplet while the hydrophilic heads stay in the water. Many soap molecules surround a droplet of grease, forming a tiny cluster called a MICELLE, with the dirt trapped at the centre. The micelles remain suspended in water and are washed away with the rinse, carrying the dirt with them.

SOAPS IN HARD WATER: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. Soap reacts with these to form an insoluble precipitate called SCUM, which wastes soap and does not clean. This is why soap does not lather well in hard water.

DETERGENTS: Detergents are synthetic cleansing agents. Their molecules also have a hydrophobic tail and a hydrophilic head, so they clean in the same way as soaps. The key DIFFERENCE is that the calcium and magnesium salts of detergents are SOLUBLE in water, so detergents do NOT form scum and work well even in HARD water. For this reason detergents are widely used in washing powders and shampoos.

SUMMARY

- Carbon is tetravalent (valency 4) and forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons; its properties of catenation and tetravalency allow it to form millions of compounds.
- Allotropes of carbon include diamond (hard, non-conductor, each C bonded to 4 others), graphite (soft, conductor, each C bonded to 3 others, layered) and fullerene (C60, football-shaped).
- Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes, CnH2n+2) have only single bonds; unsaturated hydrocarbons have double bonds (alkenes, CnH2n) or triple bonds (alkynes, CnH2n-2).
- Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures (isomerism begins at butane).
- Functional groups (-OH, -CHO, >C=O, -COOH, halo) give a compound its characteristic properties; a homologous series shares a functional group and successive members differ by -CH2-.
- Important reactions: combustion, oxidation, addition (hydrogenation of oils), substitution (in alkanes).
- Ethanol (C2H5OH) is used as a solvent and fuel; ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) gives vinegar and forms esters by esterification.
- Soaps (salts of fatty acids) clean by forming micelles but form scum in hard water; detergents are synthetic and work even in hard water.

sections.heading: Versatile nature of carbon
bullets: Carbon (Z = 6) has the configuration 2, 4 and so has four valence electrons; it neither gains nor loses electrons but SHARES them, forming covalent bonds.
Carbon is tetravalent (valency 4) - it forms four covalent bonds, as in methane CH4.
CATENATION is carbon's ability to bond with other carbon atoms to form long chains, branched chains and rings; with tetravalency this lets carbon form millions of compounds.
Carbon can also form double and triple bonds and bonds with many other elements.

sections.heading: Allotropes of carbon
bullets: Allotropes are different physical forms of the same element; carbon's main crystalline allotropes are diamond, graphite and fullerene.
In DIAMOND each carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network - it is the hardest natural substance and does not conduct electricity.
In GRAPHITE each carbon is bonded to three others in sliding layers - it is soft, used as a lubricant, and conducts electricity because the fourth electron is free.
FULLERENE (e.g. C60) consists of 60 carbon atoms arranged in a hollow football-like sphere.

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons and isomerism
bullets: A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen; saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) have only single bonds, unsaturated ones have double bonds (alkenes) or triple bonds (alkynes).
Alkanes CnH2n+2 (methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10); alkenes CnH2n (ethene C2H4); alkynes CnH2n-2 (ethyne C2H2).
IUPAC names use a prefix for the number of carbons (meth, eth, prop, but) and an ending for the family (-ane, -ene, -yne).
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures; butane (C4H10) has a straight-chain and a branched isomer.

sections.heading: Functional groups, homologous series and reactions
bullets: A functional group (-OH alcohol, -CHO aldehyde, >C=O ketone, -COOH carboxylic acid, halo) gives a compound its characteristic chemistry.
A homologous series shares one functional group and a general formula; successive members differ by a -CH2- unit and show a gradual change in physical properties.
Combustion gives CO2, water and heat; saturated hydrocarbons burn with a clean blue flame, unsaturated ones with a sooty yellow flame.
Addition reaction: unsaturated compounds add hydrogen (hydrogenation) over a nickel catalyst, used to harden vegetable oils; substitution reaction: alkanes react with chlorine in sunlight.

sections.heading: Ethanol, ethanoic acid, soaps and detergents
bullets: Ethanol (C2H5OH) is a colourless liquid used as a solvent and as a fuel (mixed with petrol as gasohol); it reacts with sodium to release hydrogen.

Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) is a weak acid; its dilute solution is vinegar and pure acid is called glacial acetic acid; it reacts with baking soda to give CO2 and with alcohols to form esters (esterification).
A soap is the sodium/potassium salt of a fatty acid; it cleans by forming MICELLES that trap grease, but forms insoluble SCUM in hard water.
Detergents are synthetic cleansers whose calcium and magnesium salts are soluble, so they work well even in hard water.

key_takeaways: Carbon shares its four valence electrons to form covalent bonds; it is tetravalent.
Catenation and tetravalency together let carbon form millions of compounds.
Diamond (hard, non-conductor), graphite (soft, conductor) and fullerene (C60) are allotropes of carbon.
Alkanes (CnH2n+2) are saturated; alkenes (CnH2n) and alkynes (CnH2n-2) are unsaturated.
A functional group gives a compound its chemistry; a homologous series differs by -CH2- between members.
Carbon compounds undergo combustion, oxidation, addition (hydrogenation) and substitution reactions.
Soaps clean by forming micelles but form scum in hard water; detergents work even in hard water.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Carbon and Its Compounds (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 28. Attempt all questions. Write balanced word equations where asked and use plain structural formulae.

questions.question: Why does carbon form covalent compounds rather than ionic ones? Explain with reference to its electronic configuration.
questions.answer: Carbon has atomic number 6 and electronic configuration 2, 4, so it has four valence electrons. To complete its octet it would have to either lose 4 electrons (forming C4+) or gain 4 electrons (forming C4-). Both require a very large amount of energy and would produce a highly charged, unstable ion. Instead, carbon SHARES its four valence electrons with other atoms, forming four covalent bonds. This sharing is energetically favourable and gives stable molecules such as methane CH4, so carbon forms covalent (not ionic) compounds.
questions.explanation: Losing or gaining 4 electrons is energetically unfavourable, so carbon shares electrons covalently.

questions.question: Compare diamond and graphite under the headings: (a) bonding/structure, (b) hardness, (c) electrical conductivity, (d) one use each.
questions.answer:
(a) Bonding/structure: In diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to FOUR other carbon atoms in a rigid three-dimensional network. In graphite each carbon is bonded to only THREE others, forming flat hexagonal layers held together by weak forces that can slide.
(b) Hardness: Diamond is the HARDEST natural substance because of its rigid 3-D network. Graphite is SOFT and slippery because its layers slide over one another.
(c) Electrical conductivity: Diamond does NOT conduct electricity (all four valence electrons are used in bonding, none free). Graphite CONDUCTS electricity because the fourth electron of each carbon is free to move.
(d) Uses: Diamond is used in cutting/drilling tools and as a gemstone; graphite is used as a lubricant and as electrodes (and in pencils).
questions.explanation: Diamond: 4 bonds, hard, non-conductor. Graphite: 3 bonds, layered, soft, conductor.

questions.question: Write the names, molecular formulae and general formulae of the first member of the alkane, alkene and alkyne families.
questions.answer:
Alkane (general formula CnH2n+2): first member is methane, CH4.
Alkene (general formula CnH2n): first member is ethene (ethylene), C2H4. (There is no one-carbon alkene because a C=C double bond needs two carbons.)
Alkyne (general formula CnH2n-2): first member is ethyne (acetylene), C2H2.
Alkanes are saturated (single bonds); alkenes have a C=C double bond; alkynes have a triple bond.
questions.explanation: Methane CH4; ethene C2H4; ethyne C2H2 with their general formulae.

questions.question: What is a homologous series? State any two characteristics.
questions.answer:
A homologous series is a family of carbon compounds that have the same general formula and the same functional group, in which each successive member differs from the previous one by a -CH2- unit (a mass of 14).
Two characteristics: (1) All members have similar CHEMICAL properties because they have the same functional group. (2) The PHYSICAL properties (such as melting and boiling points) change gradually with increasing molecular mass. (Also: they can be represented by one general formula, e.g. CnH2n+2 for alkanes.)
questions.explanation: Same general formula and functional group; successive members differ by -CH2-.

questions.question: What is hydrogenation? Give one industrial application.
questions.answer:
Hydrogenation is an ADDITION reaction in which hydrogen is added across the carbon-carbon double or triple bond of an unsaturated compound in the presence of a catalyst (nickel, palladium or platinum), converting it into a saturated compound.
Industrial application: the hardening of vegetable oils. Vegetable oils contain unsaturated carbon chains; passing hydrogen through them over a nickel catalyst converts them into solid or semi-solid fats such as vanaspati (margarine).
questions.explanation: Addition of H2 to unsaturated compounds over a Ni catalyst; hardens vegetable oils.

questions.question: Give the structural difference between a saturated and an unsaturated hydrocarbon, with one example each.
questions.answer:
A SATURATED hydrocarbon contains only single covalent bonds between carbon atoms and holds the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms; example: ethane C2H6 (an alkane).
An UNSATURATED hydrocarbon contains at least one carbon-carbon DOUBLE bond (alkene) or TRIPLE bond (alkyne); examples: ethene C2H4 (double bond) or ethyne C2H2 (triple bond).
Unsaturated hydrocarbons can undergo addition reactions, while saturated ones mainly undergo substitution.
questions.explanation: Saturated = only single bonds (ethane); unsaturated = double/triple bonds (ethene/ethyne).

questions.question: Describe the cleansing action of soap. Why does soap not work well in hard water?
questions.answer:
A soap molecule has two parts: a long hydrocarbon TAIL that is hydrophobic (water-repelling but oil-loving) and an ionic HEAD (-COONa) that is hydrophilic (water-loving).
When soap is added to water containing greasy dirt, the hydrophobic tails embed into the oil/grease while the hydrophilic heads remain in the water. Several soap molecules surround each grease droplet, forming a tiny cluster called a MICELLE, with the dirt trapped at the centre. These micelles stay suspended in water and are rinsed away, carrying the dirt with them. This is how soap cleans.
In HARD WATER (which contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts), soap reacts with these ions to form an insoluble precipitate called SCUM. The scum wastes soap and sticks to clothes, so soap does not lather or clean well in hard water.
questions.explanation: Micelle formation traps grease; in hard water soap forms insoluble scum with Ca/Mg salts.

questions.question: How will you distinguish ethanol from ethanoic acid by a simple chemical test?
questions.answer:
Add a small amount of sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda, NaHCO3) to each liquid.
- ETHANOIC ACID reacts with baking soda to give brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide gas (it is an acid): it produces CO2, water and sodium acetate.
- ETHANOL does NOT react with baking soda, so there is no effervescence.
The one that gives bubbles of gas with baking soda is ethanoic acid; the one that does not is ethanol. (Ethanoic acid also turns blue litmus red, while ethanol does not.)
questions.explanation: Ethanoic acid gives CO2 effervescence with baking soda; ethanol does not.

questions.question: What is isomerism? Draw/describe the two isomers of butane (C4H10).
questions.answer:
Isomerism is the phenomenon in which two or more compounds have the SAME molecular formula but DIFFERENT structural arrangements of atoms; such compounds are called isomers.
Butane has the molecular formula C4H10 and exists as two isomers:
 (1) n-butane (normal butane): a STRAIGHT chain of four carbon atoms, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3.
 (2) isobutane (2-methylpropane): a BRANCHED chain of three carbons with a CH3 branch on the middle carbon, (CH3)3CH.
Both have the formula C4H10 but their atoms are joined differently, giving slightly different physical properties.
questions.explanation: Same formula C4H10, different structures: straight-chain n-butane and branched isobutane.

questions.question: State two ways in which detergents differ from soaps.
questions.answer:
(1) Soaps are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids (made from natural fats and oils by saponification), whereas detergents are SYNTHETIC cleansing agents.
(2) The calcium and magnesium salts of soaps are INSOLUBLE, so soaps form scum and do not clean well in hard water; the calcium and magnesium salts of detergents are SOLUBLE, so detergents do NOT form scum and work well even in hard water.
questions.explanation: Soaps: natural salts of fatty acids, form scum in hard water. Detergents: synthetic, work in hard water.

questions.question: Carbon forms ionic bonds by losing four electrons.
questions.explanation: Carbon shares electrons (covalent), it does not form C4+ easily.

questions.question: Catenation is the ability of carbon to form chains and rings of carbon atoms.
Graphite is a good conductor of electricity.
questions.explanation: The fourth electron of each carbon is free.

questions.question: Diamond conducts electricity better than graphite.
questions.explanation: Diamond is a non-conductor; graphite conducts.

questions.question: The general formula of alkenes is CnH2n.
Alkanes are unsaturated hydrocarbons.
Methane and ethane are isomers of each other.
questions.explanation: Isomers have the same molecular formula; these differ.

questions.question: The functional group -COOH belongs to carboxylic acids.
Hydrogenation of vegetable oils converts them into solid fats.
questions.explanation: Addition of H2 over a nickel catalyst.

questions.question: Detergents form scum in hard water just like soaps.
questions.explanation: Detergent salts are soluble; they do not form scum.

questions.question: Carbon completes its octet by ____ its four valence electrons.
The valency of carbon is ____.
The self-linking of carbon atoms into chains and rings is called ____.
questions.explanation: Property unique to carbon to this extent.

questions.question: In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to ____ other carbon atoms.
The football-shaped allotrope of carbon containing 60 atoms is ____.
The general formula of alkanes is ____.
The first member of the alkyne family is ____.
The molecular formula of propane is ____.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called ____.
The functional group present in alcohols is ____.
Successive members of a homologous series differ by a ____ unit.
The chemical formula of ethanol is ____.
A dilute aqueous solution of ethanoic acid is called ____.
The reaction of an acid with an alcohol to form an ester is called ____.
The cluster of soap molecules that traps grease in water is called a ____.
Why is carbon said to be tetravalent?
questions.answer: Carbon has four electrons in its outermost shell (configuration 2, 4) and needs four more to complete its octet. It achieves this by forming four covalent bonds with other atoms, so its combining capacity (valency) is four. Because it forms four bonds, carbon is said to be tetravalent, as seen in methane CH4.
questions.explanation: Four valence electrons, four covalent bonds.

questions.question: Why does carbon not form C4+ or C4- ions?
questions.answer: To form C4+, carbon would have to lose four electrons; to form C4-, it would have to gain four electrons. Both processes need a very large amount of energy and would produce a highly charged, unstable ion. Therefore carbon avoids both routes and instead shares its electrons to form stable covalent bonds.
questions.explanation: Energetically unfavourable, so carbon shares electrons.

questions.question: State two reasons why carbon forms a very large number of compounds.
questions.answer: (1) Catenation: carbon atoms can link with one another by strong, stable covalent bonds to form long chains, branched chains and rings. (2) Tetravalency: with a valency of four, each carbon can bond to up to four other atoms, allowing complex structures. Carbon also forms double and triple bonds and bonds with many elements, further increasing the number of possible compounds.

questions.question: Explain how catenation and tetravalency together account for the millions of carbon compounds.
questions.answer: Catenation lets carbon atoms join to one another, so chains of any length, branched chains and closed rings are possible; because carbon-carbon bonds are strong and stable, even very long chains are stable. Tetravalency means each carbon has four bonding positions, so at every carbon there are several places to attach hydrogen, other carbons or functional groups. Combining a free choice of chain length and shape (from catenation) with four attachment points per carbon (from tetravalency), and adding the possibility of double and triple bonds, gives an enormous number of distinct arrangements - hence millions of compounds.
questions.explanation: Chain variety x four bonding positions x multiple bond types.

questions.question: What are allotropes? Name three allotropes of carbon.
questions.answer: Allotropes are different physical forms of the same element that have the same chemical properties but different physical properties. Three crystalline allotropes of carbon are diamond, graphite and fullerene (such as C60).

questions.question: Why is diamond hard while graphite is soft, even though both are pure carbon?
questions.answer: In diamond, every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a rigid three-dimensional network, so the atoms cannot move - this makes diamond extremely hard. In graphite, each carbon is bonded to only three others, forming flat layers; the layers are held together by weak forces and can slide over one another, which makes graphite soft and slippery. The difference in hardness comes entirely from the different arrangement of carbon atoms.
questions.explanation: Diamond: 3-D rigid network; graphite: sliding layers.

questions.question: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
questions.answer: In graphite each carbon uses only three of its four valence electrons in bonding, leaving the fourth electron free to move through the layers; these mobile electrons carry electric current, so graphite conducts. In diamond all four valence electrons of every carbon are locked into covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons and diamond does not conduct electricity.
questions.explanation: Graphite has free electrons; diamond does not.

questions.question: Write two uses each of diamond and graphite.
questions.answer: Diamond: (1) in cutting and drilling tools because it is the hardest substance; (2) as a gemstone in jewellery. Graphite: (1) as a lubricant because its layers slide easily; (2) as electrodes (and in pencil 'leads') because it conducts electricity.

questions.question: Differentiate between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
questions.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single bonds between carbon atoms and hold the maximum number of hydrogen atoms; they are the alkanes (CnH2n+2), for example ethane C2H6. Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond (alkenes, CnH2n) or triple bond (alkynes, CnH2n-2), for example ethene C2H4 or ethyne C2H2.

questions.question: Write the molecular formulae of the first four alkanes using CnH2n+2.
questions.answer: Using CnH2n+2: methane (n=1) CH4; ethane (n=2) C2H6; propane (n=3) C3H8; butane (n=4) C4H10. Each successive member has one more carbon and two more hydrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: Apply the general formula for n = 1 to 4.

questions.question: Name the alkane, alkene and alkyne with two carbon atoms and give their formulae.
questions.answer: Two-carbon alkane: ethane, C2H6 (single bond). Two-carbon alkene: ethene, C2H4 (one double bond). Two-carbon alkyne: ethyne, C2H2 (one triple bond). They differ by the type of carbon-carbon bond and hence the number of hydrogen atoms.
questions.explanation: Ethane C2H6, ethene C2H4, ethyne C2H2.

questions.question: An alkene has 4 carbon atoms. Write its molecular formula and explain.
questions.answer: An alkene follows CnH2n. With n = 4, the number of hydrogen atoms is 2 x 4 = 8, so the molecular formula is C4H8 (butene). It contains one carbon-carbon double bond, which is why it has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding alkane butane (C4H10).

questions.question: Why is ethyne (acetylene) used in welding?
questions.answer: Ethyne (C2H2) burns in oxygen with a very hot flame (the oxy-acetylene flame), reaching a high enough temperature to melt and join metals. This high-temperature flame makes ethyne suitable for welding and cutting metals.
questions.explanation: Burns with a very hot oxy-acetylene flame.

questions.question: Define isomerism and give one example.
questions.answer: Isomerism is the phenomenon in which two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements of atoms; such compounds are called isomers. For example, butane C4H10 exists as straight-chain n-butane and branched isobutane.
questions.explanation: Same molecular formula, different structure; example butane.

questions.question: Describe the two isomers of butane.
questions.answer: Butane has the molecular formula C4H10 and two structural isomers. (1) n-Butane: a straight chain of four carbon atoms, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3. (2) Isobutane (2-methylpropane): a branched chain in which three carbons form the main chain and one CH3 group branches off the middle carbon. Both have the same formula C4H10 but different structures and slightly different physical properties (such as boiling point).

questions.question: Why do methane, ethane and propane not show isomerism?
questions.answer: Isomerism requires that the same set of atoms can be arranged in more than one way. Methane (CH4), ethane (C2H6) and propane (C3H8) have too few carbon atoms to allow branching - there is only one possible way to join the carbon atoms in each. Branching (and hence isomerism) first becomes possible at four carbon atoms, so isomerism begins at butane.
questions.explanation: Too few carbons to allow a different arrangement.

questions.question: What is a functional group? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a carbon compound its characteristic chemical properties. Examples: the hydroxyl group -OH (alcohols) and the carboxyl group -COOH (carboxylic acids). Others include the aldehyde group -CHO and the halo group (-Cl, -Br).
questions.explanation: Group of atoms deciding chemistry; e.g. -OH, -COOH.

questions.question: Identify the functional group in (a) ethanol and (b) ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: (a) Ethanol (C2H5OH) contains the hydroxyl group -OH, so it is an alcohol. (b) Ethanoic acid (CH3COOH) contains the carboxyl group -COOH, so it is a carboxylic acid. The functional group in each case determines its characteristic reactions.

questions.question: What is a homologous series? List three of its characteristics.
questions.answer: A homologous series is a family of carbon compounds having the same general formula and the same functional group, in which successive members differ by a -CH2- unit. Characteristics: (1) all members can be represented by one general formula (e.g. CnH2n+2 for alkanes); (2) successive members differ by -CH2- (a mass of 14); (3) members have similar chemical properties (same functional group) but show a gradual change in physical properties such as boiling point with increasing molecular mass.
questions.explanation: Same general formula and functional group; differ by -CH2-; gradual physical change.

questions.question: Two successive members of a homologous series differ in molar mass by how much, and why?
questions.answer: They differ by 14 units. Each successive member has one extra carbon atom and two extra hydrogen atoms, that is an additional -CH2- group. The mass of -CH2- is 12 (carbon) + 2 x 1 (hydrogen) = 14, so consecutive members differ in molar mass by 14.

questions.question: What happens when a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion?
questions.answer: In complete combustion a hydrocarbon burns in plenty of oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water vapour, releasing a large amount of heat (and usually light). For example, methane burns as CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat. This is why hydrocarbons are used as fuels.

questions.question: Distinguish between an addition reaction and a substitution reaction.
questions.answer: In an addition reaction an atom or molecule (such as hydrogen) adds across the double or triple bond of an unsaturated compound, converting it into a saturated compound; for example hydrogenation of an alkene. In a substitution reaction an atom in a saturated compound (such as a hydrogen of an alkane) is replaced by another atom; for example methane reacting with chlorine in sunlight (CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl).
questions.explanation: Addition: across multiple bond; substitution: one atom replaces another.

questions.question: What is hydrogenation of oils, and what is it used for?
questions.answer: Hydrogenation of oils is an addition reaction in which hydrogen gas is passed through vegetable oil in the presence of a nickel catalyst. The hydrogen adds across the double bonds of the unsaturated oil, converting it into a saturated solid or semi-solid fat. It is used to make vanaspati (margarine) from liquid vegetable oils.
questions.explanation: H2 added to unsaturated oil over Ni; makes vanaspati.

questions.question: List three uses of ethanol.
questions.answer: Ethanol is used: (1) as a solvent in medicines (tinctures), perfumes and many industrial products; (2) as a fuel - it is blended with petrol to make gasohol and burns to give carbon dioxide, water and heat; (3) as a raw material for making other chemicals such as ethanoic acid and esters. (It is also the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, though it is harmful in excess.)

questions.question: Describe two important reactions of ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: (1) Reaction with a base/carbonate: ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda) to give carbon dioxide gas, water and sodium acetate; the brisk effervescence of CO2 is a test for the acid. (2) Esterification: ethanoic acid reacts with an alcohol (such as ethanol) in the presence of a little concentrated acid to form a sweet-smelling ester and water. Ethanoic acid is also a weak acid and turns blue litmus red.
questions.explanation: Reaction with baking soda (CO2) and esterification with alcohol.

questions.question: Explain why ethanol is being promoted as a fuel, and give one drawback of consuming it.
questions.answer: Ethanol burns cleanly to give carbon dioxide and water, releasing heat, and it can be produced from renewable plant material (such as sugarcane). Blending ethanol with petrol (gasohol) reduces the use of fossil fuel and gives cleaner combustion with fewer pollutants, so it is promoted as a fuel. Drawback of consumption: ethanol affects the central nervous system; drinking it (especially in excess) is harmful to health and impairs judgement and coordination.
questions.explanation: Renewable, clean-burning fuel; but harmful to the nervous system when consumed.

questions.question: What is soap, and how is it made?
questions.answer: A soap is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid (a carboxylic acid). It is made by heating a fat or oil with sodium hydroxide; this reaction, which produces soap and glycerol, is called saponification.
questions.explanation: Salt of a fatty acid; made by saponification of fat with alkali.

questions.question: Explain the cleansing action of soap using the idea of a micelle.
questions.answer: A soap molecule has a long hydrophobic (water-repelling, oil-loving) hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head. In greasy water the tails dissolve into the grease while the heads stay in the water. Many soap molecules surround each grease droplet to form a cluster called a micelle, with the dirt trapped at the centre and the heads pointing outward into the water. The micelles stay suspended and are washed away during rinsing, removing the dirt.
questions.explanation: Tails enter grease, heads stay in water, forming micelles that wash away.

questions.question: Why does soap form scum in hard water but detergent does not?
questions.answer: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. Soap (a salt of a fatty acid) reacts with these ions to form an insoluble precipitate called scum, which wastes soap and does not clean. Detergents are synthetic, and their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble in water, so they do not form scum and continue to clean effectively even in hard water.
questions.explanation: Soap's Ca/Mg salts are insoluble (scum); detergent's are soluble.

questions.question: Define an allotrope and explain why diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
questions.answer: Allotropes are two or more different physical forms of the same element that have the same chemical properties but different physical properties. Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms and react chemically the same way (both burn to give carbon dioxide), but they have very different physical properties because their carbon atoms are arranged differently - diamond in a rigid 3-D network and graphite in sliding layers. Hence they are allotropes of carbon.
questions.explanation: Same element and chemistry, different physical arrangement.

questions.question: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, yet diamond is the hardest known substance and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft, slippery and conducts electricity. Fullerene (C60) is a third form shaped like a football. (a) What name is given to such different forms of one element? (b) How many carbon atoms is each carbon bonded to in diamond and in graphite? (c) Why does graphite conduct electricity? (d) Give one use of graphite based on its softness.
questions.answer: (a) They are called allotropes (the phenomenon is allotropy). (b) In diamond each carbon is bonded to 4 other carbon atoms; in graphite each carbon is bonded to 3 other carbon atoms. (c) In graphite the fourth valence electron of each carbon is free to move through the layers, and these mobile electrons carry electric current, so graphite conducts. (d) Because its layers slide over one another, graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant (and in pencils).
questions.explanation: Tests allotropy, bonding numbers, conductivity and a use of graphite.

questions.question: The alkanes form a homologous series with general formula CnH2n+2. The first four are methane, ethane, propane and butane. (a) Write the molecular formula of propane. (b) Write the molecular formula of butane. (c) State the general formula of alkenes. (d) How does an alkene differ structurally from an alkane?
questions.answer: (a) Propane (n = 3): C3H8. (b) Butane (n = 4): C4H10. (c) The general formula of alkenes is CnH2n. (d) An alkane has only single carbon-carbon bonds (saturated), whereas an alkene contains at least one carbon-carbon double bond (unsaturated), so an alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding alkane.
questions.explanation: Applies CnH2n+2 and compares alkanes with alkenes.

questions.question: A student takes two test tubes, one containing ethanol and the other ethanoic acid. To each she adds a pinch of sodium hydrogen carbonate (baking soda). Brisk bubbling is seen in only one tube. (a) Which tube shows bubbling? (b) Name the gas evolved. (c) Write the products of this reaction in words. (d) Suggest one more test to identify ethanoic acid.
questions.answer: (a) The tube containing ethanoic acid shows brisk bubbling. (b) The gas evolved is carbon dioxide. (c) Ethanoic acid + sodium hydrogen carbonate -> sodium acetate + water + carbon dioxide. (d) Another test: ethanoic acid turns blue litmus paper red (it is an acid), whereas ethanol has no effect on litmus; alternatively, ethanoic acid has a sharp vinegar-like smell.
questions.explanation: Distinguishes ethanol from ethanoic acid by the baking-soda test.

questions.question: In a village the water is hard. People notice that soap does not lather well and a sticky white solid forms on their clothes, wasting a lot of soap. A shopkeeper suggests using detergent instead. (a) Name the sticky solid formed. (b) Which dissolved salts in the water cause this? (c) Why does detergent work better here? (d) Name the structure soap forms around grease.
questions.answer: (a) The sticky solid is scum. (b) Dissolved calcium and magnesium salts (which make the water hard) cause it. (c) Detergents work better because their calcium and magnesium salts are soluble in water, so they do not form scum and clean effectively even in hard water. (d) Soap forms a structure called a micelle around the grease.
questions.explanation: Connects hard water, scum, detergents and micelles.

questions.question: Carbon (Z = 6) has the electronic configuration 2, 4. Instead of forming ions, carbon forms compounds such as methane (CH4) and carbon tetrachloride (CCl4). (a) How many valence electrons does carbon have? (b) Why does carbon not form C4+ or C4- ions? (c) What type of bond does carbon form? (d) How many bonds does carbon form in CCl4?
questions.answer: (a) Carbon has 4 valence electrons. (b) Forming C4+ (losing 4 electrons) or C4- (gaining 4 electrons) would need a very large amount of energy and give an unstable, highly charged ion, so carbon avoids both. (c) Carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons. (d) In CCl4 carbon forms 4 covalent bonds, one to each chlorine atom.
questions.explanation: Covers valence electrons, why no ions form, covalency and bond count.

questions.question: Butane and isobutane both have the molecular formula C4H10, but butane is a straight chain while isobutane is branched. They have slightly different boiling points. (a) What is the name for compounds like these? (b) What is the phenomenon called? (c) From which alkane does this phenomenon first appear? (d) Why can propane not show it?
questions.answer: (a) They are called isomers. (b) The phenomenon is called isomerism (structural isomerism). (c) It first appears at butane (C4H10). (d) Propane has only three carbon atoms, which can be joined in just one way, so no different arrangement (no branching) is possible and it cannot show isomerism.
questions.explanation: Tests isomers, isomerism and why it begins at butane.

questions.question: Consider the alcohols: methanol (CH3OH), ethanol (C2H5OH) and propanol (C3H7OH). Each contains the same functional group, and they show similar chemical properties but a steady rise in boiling point. (a) Name the functional group they share. (b) What is such a family of compounds called? (c) By what unit do successive members differ? (d) Why do their chemical properties stay similar?
questions.answer: (a) They share the hydroxyl group, -OH. (b) Such a family is called a homologous series. (c) Successive members differ by a -CH2- unit (a mass of 14). (d) Their chemical properties stay similar because they all contain the same functional group (-OH), which determines the chemical behaviour of a carbon compound.
questions.explanation: Covers functional group, homologous series, -CH2- and similar chemistry.

questions.question: Liquid vegetable oils contain unsaturated carbon chains. In a factory, hydrogen gas is passed through the oil in the presence of nickel, and the oil turns into a solid fat used as vanaspati. (a) What is this reaction called? (b) What type of reaction (addition or substitution) is it? (c) Why is nickel used? (d) Why does the oil become solid?
questions.answer: (a) The reaction is called hydrogenation. (b) It is an addition reaction (hydrogen is added across the double bonds). (c) Nickel is used as a catalyst, to speed up the reaction. (d) Adding hydrogen across the double bonds converts the unsaturated oil into a saturated fat, which is solid (or semi-solid) at room temperature, giving vanaspati.
questions.explanation: Applies hydrogenation/addition and the role of the nickel catalyst.

questions.question: Silicon, like carbon, has four valence electrons, yet silicon forms only a small number of compounds while carbon forms millions. (a) Name the property by which carbon links to itself. (b) Why does carbon form so many more compounds than silicon? (c) Name two shapes of carbon skeletons made possible by this property. (d) State the valency of carbon.
questions.answer: (a) The property is catenation. (b) Carbon shows catenation to a very large extent because carbon-carbon bonds are strong and stable, so very long and varied chains can form; silicon-silicon bonds are weaker, so silicon catenates only slightly and forms far fewer compounds. (c) Two shapes: long/branched chains and closed rings. (d) The valency of carbon is 4 (tetravalent).
questions.explanation: Compares carbon and silicon catenation; covers chain shapes and valency.

questions.question: Pencils are said to contain 'lead', but they actually contain graphite, an allotrope of carbon. Diamond is another allotrope of the same element. (a) What is an allotrope? (b) Why can graphite mark paper while diamond cannot? (c) Which of the two conducts electricity? (d) Name one allotrope of carbon shaped like a football.
questions.answer: (a) An allotrope is one of two or more physical forms of the same element with the same chemical but different physical properties. (b) Graphite has layers held by weak forces that slide off easily and rub onto the paper, so it can write; diamond is a hard rigid network and cannot. (c) Graphite conducts electricity (diamond does not). (d) Fullerene (C60) is shaped like a football.
questions.explanation: Everyday context for allotropy, graphite layers, conductivity and fullerene.
